pll1d23c1-d1e3503.summary: Notes that while all substantial names are said singularly of the persons in sum, 'person' is an exception: said of each according to substance (the Father is a person, etc.), it is taken plurally in sum, 'three persons,' not 'one person.'
claims: 'Person' is said substantially of each person.
'Person' is said plurally of the three.

pll1d23c1-d1e3506.summary: Shows from De Trinitate VII that 'person' is said according to substance: for God being and being a person are wholly the same.
claims: For God, to be and to be a person are the same.

pll1d23c1-d1e3526.summary: Further De Trinitate VII: 'person of the Father' means nothing other than the Father's substance; as the Father's substance is the Father, by which he is, not by which he is Father, so his person is the Father, said 'ad se,' like God, great, good, just.
claims: 'Person of the Father' means the substance of the Father.

pll1d23c1-d1e3538.summary: Concludes that 'person' is said according to substance, so 'the Father is a person' means 'the Father is the divine essence,' and likewise for Son and Spirit.
claims: 'The Father is a person' means 'the Father is the divine essence.'

pll1d23c1-d1e3543.summary: Raises a difficult but useful question: why are the three not called one person, as they are one essence and one God?

pll1d23c1-d1e3546.summary: Gives Augustine's answer from De Trinitate VII and V: we say three persons, though not three gods or essences, so as to keep one word for what we understand by Trinity, lest we be wholly silent when asked 'three what?' Human speech labors in great poverty; 'three persons' was said not to express it but so as not to remain silent, since the eminence of the ineffable cannot be explained by this word.
claims: 'Three persons' is said to answer 'three what?'
Human language is impoverished before the Trinity.
The word 'person' does not express the ineffable reality.
concepts: non ut diceretur sed ne taceretur

pll1d23c1-d1e3582.summary: Concludes that 'persons' is said plurally by necessity, so that by this one name we can answer those asking about the three.
claims: 'Persons' is said plurally out of necessity of answering.

pl-l1d23c1.summary: Notes an exception to the rule that substantial names are said singularly of the three in sum: 'person' is said of each person according to substance (with Augustine, for God to be is to be a person, and 'person of the Father' means the Father's substance), yet in sum it is said plurally, 'three persons,' not 'one person.' Why not 'one person' as 'one essence'? Augustine: so that, asked 'three what?', we would have one word for what we confess to be three. 'Three persons' was said not to express the ineffable but so as not to remain silent.
claims: 'Person' is said of each divine person according to substance.
For God, to be is to be a person; 'person' is said 'ad se.'
Unlike other substantial names, 'person' is said plurally in sum: three persons.
'Three persons' is said out of the poverty of language, so as not to be silent when asked 'three what?'
The eminence of the ineffable thing cannot be expressed by this word.
